title: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Auditory Perception” (from p. 585), p. 586. Scope: human auditory perception of sounds generated from discrete sequences

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Auditory behavioral data can test restricted classes, and the claim has clear counterexamples in principle. Existing public coverage is unlikely to support the exhaustive scope implied by 'essentially nothing else.'

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Synthesize sounds from sequences matched on spectrum but differing in repetition, nesting, and other algorithmic structure, then measure discrimination and structure reports. Reliable perception of non-repetitive structure after spectral controls would refute the 'essentially nothing else' claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Spectral peaks and temporal structure are difficult to match independently.

Listeners differ with musical training.

Existing datasets may not use the required matched synthetic sequences.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.7

discriminating power: 0.58
data adequacy: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Pitch and the hearing of periodic sounds are heavily measured, which covers the positive half of the claim. The negative half, that nested or other non-repetitive structure is heard as noise, needs stimuli built from discrete sequences of the kind Wolfram considers. Those comparisons exist mainly as scattered studies, not as a dataset matched to the claim's scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Synthesize sounds from sequences that are periodic, nested, or otherwise non-repetitive but spectrally matched, and test whether listeners identify structure beyond pitch and a few spectral peaks. Identification limited to repetition at definite frequencies would support the claim; reliable detection of nested or other non-repetitive structure would refute 'essentially nothing else'.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sounds that carry nested structure are scarce in existing listening-test archives.

Listeners also report timbre, envelope, and speech-like structure, so the stimulus class 'fairly uniform sequences' has to be enforced.

data existence: 0.5
